claim: A human expressed sequence tag (EST) exists in which L1CAM exon 25 is excluded from the mature mRNA.
source: A bioinformatics analysis with the ExonMine program (http://www.imm.fm.ul.pt/exonmine/) (Mollet et al., 2010) identified a human expressed sequence tag (EST) in which the L1CAM exon 25 (a 135-nucleotide cassette exon) is excluded from the mature mRNA (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by bioinformatics analysis using the ExonMine program, which identified an EST showing exon 25 exclusion.

claim: L1CAM exon 25 is a 135-nucleotide cassette exon.
source: A bioinformatics analysis with the ExonMine program (http://www.imm.fm.ul.pt/exonmine/) (Mollet et al., 2010) identified a human expressed sequence tag (EST) in which the L1CAM exon 25 (a 135-nucleotide cassette exon) is excluded from the mature mRNA (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the bioinformatics analysis.

claim: Skipping of L1CAM exon 25 mainly occurs in endothelial cells in both human and mouse samples.
source: As shown in Figure 1B and C, in both human and mouse samples the skipping of exon 25 mainly occurred in ECs.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 1B and C comparing various tissues and EC lines.

claim: Endothelial cells express a novel alternatively spliced isoform of L1CAM devoid of exon 25.
source: Overall, these data suggest that ECs express a novel alternatively spliced isoform of L1CAM devoid of exon 25.
evidence: The claim is based on RT-PCR data showing exon 25 skipping predominantly in ECs.

claim: Skipping of exon 25 results in an in-frame deletion of a 44-amino acid sequence in mouse L1CAM that encompasses the entire transmembrane domain.
source: Skipping of exon 25 results in an in-frame deletion of a 44-amino acid sequence (45 in mouse) that encompasses the entire transmembrane (TM) domain of L1CAM (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: L1-FL is prominently exposed on the cell surface of moEC.
source: Only L1-FL was prominently exposed on the cell surface of moEC, while cells expressing L1-ΔTM exhibited mainly a cytoplasmic localization (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 2C.

claim: L1-ΔTM exhibits mainly a cytoplasmic localization in moEC.
source: Only L1-FL was prominently exposed on the cell surface of moEC, while cells expressing L1-ΔTM exhibited mainly a cytoplasmic localization (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Conditioned medium from L1-ΔTM-expressing moEC contains high amounts of L1-ΔTM.
source: Indeed, conditioned medium (CM) from L1-ΔTM-expressing moEC contained high amounts of L1-ΔTM (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting of conditioned medium shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The L1-ΔTM protein in the conditioned medium retains the cytoplasmic tail.
source: Of note, the protein in the CM retained the cytoplasmic tail (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting with antibodies against the cytoplasmic domain shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: L1-ΔTM release represents the release of the entire molecule as opposed to proteolytic cleavage of full-length L1CAM.
source: This confirmed the release of the entire molecule as opposed to the proteolytic cleavage of full-length L1CAM, which results in the shedding of its extracellular portion (Figure 2D; Mechtersheimer et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 2D and comparison with known proteolytic cleavage mechanisms cited from Mechtersheimer et al., 2001.

claim: L1-ΔTM is detected in the culture medium as a single band that migrates slower than the protein found in the cell lysate.
source: Interestingly, L1-ΔTM was detected in the culture medium as a single band that migrated slower than the protein found in the cell lysate (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The different size of L1-ΔTM in culture medium versus cell lysate is accounted for by the glycosylation state of the protein.
source: We hypothesized that the different size was accounted for by the glycosylation state of the protein. This was confirmed by the forced expression of L1-ΔTM in N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase I-deficient HEK293 cells [GnTI(-)] (Reeves et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by experiments in GnTI(-) cells showing altered molecular weight, confirming glycosylation differences.

claim: L1-ΔTM is released in its mature, fully glycosylated form.
source: These findings support the notion that L1-ΔTM is released in its mature, fully glycosylated form.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the glycosylation experiments in GnTI(-) cells.

claim: lu2EC express relatively high levels of L1cam.
source: In order to confirm the release of endothelial L1-ΔTM in an endogenous system, we employed lu2EC, an immortalized mouse endothelial cell line that expresses relatively high levels of L1cam (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by expression data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: lu2EC express endogenous L1-ΔTM.
source: These cells also express endogenous L1-ΔTM (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: High levels of L1-ΔTM are found in lu2EC-derived conditioned medium.
source: When the lu2EC-derived CM was immunoblotted with the antibody against the cytoplasmic tail of L1CAM, we found high levels of L1-ΔTM (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), confirming its release into the extracellular space.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting of conditioned medium shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: B16 melanoma cells express high levels of endogenous L1CAM.
source: To compare our findings in ECs with a non-endothelial cell type, we used the mouse melanoma cell line B16, which also expresses high levels of endogenous L1CAM (Linnemann and Bock, 1986; Magrini et al., 2014), but does not express L1-ΔTM (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Linnemann and Bock, 1986 and Magrini et al., 2014, and data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: B16 melanoma cells do not express L1-ΔTM.
source: To compare our findings in ECs with a non-endothelial cell type, we used the mouse melanoma cell line B16, which also expresses high levels of endogenous L1CAM (Linnemann and Bock, 1986; Magrini et al., 2014), but does not express L1-ΔTM (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: No C-terminus-containing L1CAM is detected in the conditioned medium of B16 cells.
source: While we could detect high levels of cell-associated L1CAM, no C-terminus-containing L1CAM was detected in the CM of B16 cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), supporting the hypothesis that the AS of L1CAM results in the release of L1-ΔTM in ECs.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting of B16 conditioned medium shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Skipping of L1CAM exon 25 generates a novel isoform of the protein that is released in the extracellular compartment.
source: Collectively, our results indicate that skipping of L1CAM exon 25 generates a novel isoform of the protein that is released in the extracellular compartment.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on multiple experimental results showing L1-ΔTM release.

claim: L1-ΔTM enhances significantly the tube forming ability of moEC.
source: As shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3A and Video 1, L1-ΔTM enhanced significantly the tube forming ability of moEC, thus suggesting that it is endowed with angiogenic properties.
evidence: The claim is supported by tube formation assay data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: L1-ΔTM is endowed with angiogenic properties.
source: As shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3A and Video 1, L1-ΔTM enhanced significantly the tube forming ability of moEC, thus suggesting that it is endowed with angiogenic properties.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the enhanced tube formation ability of L1-ΔTM-expressing cells.

claim: Anti-L1CAM antibody 324 abolishes the tube-forming potential of moEC expressing L1-ΔTM.
source: As shown in Figure 3B, the antibody 324, but not a control antibody, abolished the tube-forming potential of moEC.
evidence: The claim is supported by tube formation assay with neutralizing antibody shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Neutralization of vascular L1-ΔTM is a potential strategy to interfere with the angiogenic process.
source: The results of this proof-of-concept experiment also support the neutralization of vascular L1-ΔTM as a potential strategy to interfere with the angiogenic process.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the antibody neutralization experiment showing abolished tube formation.

claim: Parental moEC treated with conditioned medium from L1-ΔTM-expressing moEC exhibit higher tube-forming activity than those exposed to control medium.
source: ECs exposed to the CM from L1-ΔTM-expressing cells exhibited higher tube-forming activity than those exposed to control medium (Figure 3C) or to the CM from L1-FL-expressing cells (not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by tube formation assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Recombinant soluble L1-ΔTM induces moEC tube formation in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Indeed, recombinant soluble L1-ΔTM induced moEC tube formation in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 3D), thus confirming its ability to stimulate EC remodeling and morphogenesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by tube formation assay with recombinant protein shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Treatment with a morpholino oligonucleotide that selectively prevents the inclusion of L1cam exon 25 results in increased expression and extracellular release of endogenous L1-ΔTM in lu2EC.
source: In order to validate our results in an EC model with endogenous L1-ΔTM, we treated lu2EC with a morpholino oligonucleotide that selectively prevents the inclusion of L1cam exon 25 (Figure 3E). As shown in Figure 3F, this resulted in increased expression and extracellular release of endogenous L1-ΔTM.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR and immunoblotting data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: lu2EC exposed to conditioned medium from morpholino-treated cells exhibit higher tube-forming activity than those exposed to control conditioned medium.
source: Importantly, lu2EC exposed to the CM from morpholino-treated cells exhibited higher tube-forming activity than those exposed to control CM, thus confirming the functionality of endogenous L1-ΔTM (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by tube formation assay data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Neovascularization is markedly induced by L1-ΔTM-containing conditioned medium in Matrigel plugs implanted in mice.
source: Neovascularization was markedly induced by L1-ΔTM-containing CM, while a weaker effect was observed with the CM from L1-FL-expressing cells (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo Matrigel plug assay data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: L1-ΔTM has angiogenic function in vivo.
source: This strongly supports the angiogenic function of L1-ΔTM.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the in vivo Matrigel plug assay showing increased neovascularization.

claim: Treating parental moEC with recombinant L1-ΔTM results in increased phospho-FGFR1.
source: As shown in Figure 3H, treating parental moEC with recombinant L1-ΔTM resulted in increased phospho-FGFR1, consistent with the L1-ΔTM-induced activation of FGFR1 signaling.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting for phospho-FGFR1 shown in Figure 3H.

claim: L1-ΔTM induces activation of FGFR1 signaling.
source: As shown in Figure 3H, treating parental moEC with recombinant L1-ΔTM resulted in increased phospho-FGFR1, consistent with the L1-ΔTM-induced activation of FGFR1 signaling.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the increased FGFR1 phosphorylation upon L1-ΔTM treatment.

claim: FGFR1 inhibitor PD173074 reduces L1-ΔTM-dependent tube-forming activity to the level of control cells.
source: Moreover, when L1-ΔTM-expressing moEC were subjected to tube formation assay in the presence of the small-molecule FGFR1 inhibitor PD173074 (Skaper et al., 2000), L1-ΔTM-dependent tube-forming activity was reduced to the level of control cells (Figure 3I).
evidence: The claim is supported by tube formation assay with FGFR1 inhibitor shown in Figure 3I.

claim: FGFR1 signaling is an effector of L1-ΔTM in endothelial cells.
source: Thus, our data implicate FGFR1 signaling as an effector of L1-ΔTM in ECs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the FGFR1 phosphorylation and inhibitor experiments.

claim: Clustered and evolutionarily conserved putative binding sites for NOVA2, hnRNP A1 and SRSF3 were identified in the L1cam exon 25 region.
source: This analysis resulted in the identification of clustered and evolutionarily conserved putative binding sites for NOVA2, hnRNP A1 and SRSF3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), three factors previously reported to be expressed in ECs (Giampietro et al., 2015; Holly et al., 2013; Lomnytska et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by bioinformatics analysis using SFmap and citations to prior work.

claim: Skipping of L1cam exon 25 in the minigene is only observed upon overexpression of NOVA2.
source: As shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1, skipping of L1cam exon 25 in the minigene was only observed upon overexpression of NOVA2, a key regulator of AS in ECs (Giampietro et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by minigene splicing assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Overexpression of hnRNP A1 and SRSF3 has no effect on the skipping of L1cam exon 25.
source: In contrast, the overexpression of hnRNP A1 and SRSF3 had no effect on the skipping of exon 25, suggesting that the latter is a NOVA2-specific effect.
evidence: The claim is supported by minigene splicing assay data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mutations in five YCAY repeats (Mut5) decrease skipping of L1cam exon 25 caused by NOVA2 overexpression.
source: We found that mutations in only three repeats (Mut3) had a limited effect, whereas mutations in five repeats (Mut5) decreased skipping of L1cam exon 25 caused by NOVA2 overexpression (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by minigene splicing assay with mutated NOVA2 binding sites shown in Figure 4C.

claim: L1cam exon 25 emerged as a novel NOVA2 target in endothelial cells from RNA-seq data in NOVA2-knockdown ECs.
source: L1cam exon 25 emerged as a novel NOVA2 target in ECs from the RNA-seq data in NOVA2-knockdown ECs (Giampietro et al., 2015) (Supplementary file 2) (see Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq analysis of NOVA2-knockdown cells.

claim: Forced expression of NOVA2 increases skipping of L1cam exon 25 in moEC.
source: In particular, forced expression of NOVA2 increased skipping of L1cam exon 25 (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR data from NOVA2-overexpressing moEC shown in Figure 4E.

claim: In NOVA2-depleted moEC, the skipping of L1cam exon 25 is markedly reduced.
source: Conversely, in NOVA2-depleted moEC (Figure 4—figure supplement 3) the skipping of L1cam exon 25 was markedly reduced (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR data from NOVA2-knockdown moEC shown in Figure 4F.

claim: NOVA2-mediated alternative splicing regulation of L1cam exon 25 is confirmed in lu2EC.
source: The NOVA2-mediated AS regulation of L1cam exon 25 was also confirmed in lu2EC, another murine EC line (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data in lu2EC shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The YCAY cluster in L1cam exon 25 is conserved between mouse and human with six repeats present in the human sequence.
source: Notably, the YCAY cluster is conserved between mouse and human L1CAM exons 25 with six repeats present in the human sequence (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: NOVA2 overexpression promotes skipping of L1CAM exon 25 in human endothelial cells.
source: Accordingly, NOVA2 overexpression promotes skipping of L1CAM exon 25 also in human ECs (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR data from human ECs shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: NOVA2 binds to the endogenous L1cam transcript at the level of exon 25.
source: As shown in Figure 4G, NOVA2 bound to the endogenous L1cam transcript at the level of exon 25, while we observed no binding with either exon or intron 26.
evidence: The claim is supported by CLIP assay data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: NOVA2 directly and specifically interacts with L1cam exon 25.
source: These data indicated a direct and specific interaction of NOVA2 with L1cam exon 25.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the CLIP data showing NOVA2 binding to exon 25 but not to exons or introns 26.

claim: NOVA2 is not involved in the alternative splicing of L1cam exons 2 and 27 in endothelial cells.
source: NOVA2 has been implicated also in the inclusion of exons 2 and 27 in neural cells (Mikulak et al., 2012). However, both RT-PCR and CLIP data showed no involvement of NOVA2 in the AS of these two exons in ECs (Figure 4G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1), further supporting the specific effect of NOVA2 on exon 25 in this cell type.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR and CLIP data shown in Figure 4G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: NOVA2 promotes skipping of L1cam exon 25 by binding to the YCAY motifs located within this exon.
source: Collectively, our results support the notion that NOVA2 promotes skipping of L1cam exon 25 by binding to the YCAY motifs located within this exon.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on minigene, mutation, and CLIP experiments.

claim: There is a markedly higher number of NOVA2-positive vessels in ovarian carcinoma than in healthy ovaries.
source: In fact, we found a markedly higher number of NOVA2-positive vessels in OC (identified via staining with the endothelial marker CD31) than in healthy ovaries (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The percentage of L1CAM-positive vessels is dramatically increased in ovarian carcinoma samples as compared to normal ovary.
source: The percentage of L1CAM-positive vessels was also dramatically increased in OC samples as compared to normal ovary (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: NOVA2 is often co-expressed with L1CAM in ovarian carcinoma vessels.
source: In addition, NOVA2 was often co-expressed with L1CAM in OC vessels (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The L1-ΔTM isoform is readily detected in endothelial cells isolated from ovarian carcinoma.
source: Thus, we applied RT-PCR to examine the AS of L1CAM in ECs isolated from OC (HOC-EC). As shown in Figure 5C, the L1-ΔTM isoform was readily detected in HOC-EC from seven independent OC samples.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: A significantly higher vessel density is found in L1-ΔTM-positive ovarian carcinoma tumors.
source: To test whether vascular L1-ΔTM in OC is associated with tumor angiogenesis, we measured the vessel density in a small cohort of OC samples pre-classified as L1-ΔTM-positive or negative by RT-qPCR (Figure 5—figure supplement 2). A significantly higher vessel density was found in L1-ΔTM-positive tumors (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by vessel density measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Among L1-ΔTM-positive tumors, the levels of L1-ΔTM correlate with vessel density.
source: Furthermore, among the tumors which exhibited L1-ΔTM expression, the levels of L1-ΔTM correlated with vessel density (r = 0.7671; p<0.01), measured by CD31 immunostaining (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The alternative splicing of L1CAM correlates with the degree of ovarian carcinoma vascularization.
source: These findings imply that the AS of L1CAM correlates with the degree of OC vascularization, which is consistent with a proangiogenic function of L1-ΔTM in this tumor type.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the correlation between L1-ΔTM levels and vessel density.

claim: Higher expression of NOVA2 correlates with shorter overall survival of ovarian carcinoma patients.
source: As shown in Figure 5E, higher expression of NOVA2 correlated with shorter overall survival of the patients (HR: 1.486; p=0.003).
evidence: The claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 5E using TCGA data.

claim: NOVA2 promotes alternative splicing of the L1CAM pre-mRNA in ovarian carcinoma vessels.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that NOVA2 promotes AS of the L1CAM pre-mRNA in OC vessels, thus accounting for the vascular expression of L1-ΔTM, and highlight the proangiogenic role and the prognostic value of the NOVA2/L1-ΔTM axis in OC.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the co-expression of NOVA2 and L1-ΔTM in OC vessels and their association with vascularization and survival.

claim: L1-ΔTM is a novel, endothelial cell-derived angiogenic factor.
source: Our results point to L1-ΔTM as a novel, EC-derived angiogenic factor which may represent a target for innovative antiangiogenic therapies.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on the angiogenic activity of L1-ΔTM demonstrated in multiple assays.

claim: L1CAM is a cell surface glycoprotein with an extracellular portion that comprises six Ig-like domains, five fibronectin type III repeats, a short transmembrane domain, and a conserved cytoplasmic tail.
source: L1CAM, also known as CD171 or L1, is a cell adhesion molecule encoded by the gene L1CAM. It is a cell surface glycoprotein with an extracellular portion that comprises six Ig-like domains, five fibronectin type III repeats, a short transmembrane (TM) domain, and a conserved cytoplasmic tail.
evidence: The claim is a description of L1CAM structure based on established knowledge.

claim: ADAM10-mediated cleavage at membrane proximal site induces shedding of the L1CAM ectodomain.
source: A disintegrin and metalloproteinase (ADAM)10-mediated cleavage at membrane proximal site induces shedding of the L1CAM ectodomain (Mechtersheimer et al., 2001), while intramembrane processing mediated by γ-secretase generates a cytosolic domain which can translocate to the nucleus and modulate gene expression (Maretzky et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Mechtersheimer et al., 2001.

claim: Intramembrane processing mediated by γ-secretase generates a cytosolic domain of L1CAM which can translocate to the nucleus and modulate gene expression.
source: A disintegrin and metalloproteinase (ADAM)10-mediated cleavage at membrane proximal site induces shedding of the L1CAM ectodomain (Mechtersheimer et al., 2001), while intramembrane processing mediated by γ-secretase generates a cytosolic domain which can translocate to the nucleus and modulate gene expression (Maretzky et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Maretzky et al., 2005.

claim: L1CAM was initially identified in the nervous system and characterized for its important function in neural development and plasticity.
source: L1CAM was initially identified in the nervous system and characterized for its important function in neural development and plasticity (Maness and Schachner, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Maness and Schachner, 2007.

claim: L1CAM is expressed in the tumor vasculature of several cancer types.
source: Further studies then showed that L1CAM is not restricted to the nervous system and, in particular, we reported its expression in the tumor vasculature of several cancer types, while no or very low L1CAM expression is detectable in normal vessels (Maddaluno et al., 2009; Magrini et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Maddaluno et al., 2009 and Magrini et al., 2014.

claim: No or very low L1CAM expression is detectable in normal vessels.
source: Further studies then showed that L1CAM is not restricted to the nervous system and, in particular, we reported its expression in the tumor vasculature of several cancer types, while no or very low L1CAM expression is detectable in normal vessels (Maddaluno et al., 2009; Magrini et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Maddaluno et al., 2009 and Magrini et al., 2014.

claim: L1CAM orchestrates different endothelial cell functions within tumor-associated vessels, such as permeability, pericyte coverage and polarity.
source: L1CAM orchestrates different endothelial cell (EC) functions within tumor-associated vessels, such as permeability, pericyte coverage and polarity.
evidence: The claim is based on prior research on L1CAM function in tumor vessels.

claim: L1CAM has emerged as a potential target for tumor vascular-specific therapies.
source: Since these cellular processes influence tumor angiogenesis, cancer growth and metastasis, L1CAM has emerged as a potential target for tumor vascular-specific therapies (Magrini et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Magrini et al., 2014.

claim: Neurons typically express the full-length variant of L1CAM.
source: L1CAM occurs mainly in two alternatively spliced isoforms: while neurons typically express the full-length variant of L1CAM, non-neural cell types produce a shorter isoform which lacks exon 2 and exon 27.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about L1CAM isoforms.

claim: Non-neural cell types produce a shorter L1CAM isoform which lacks exon 2 and exon 27.
source: L1CAM occurs mainly in two alternatively spliced isoforms: while neurons typically express the full-length variant of L1CAM, non-neural cell types produce a shorter isoform which lacks exon 2 and exon 27.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about L1CAM isoforms.

claim: L1CAM exon 2 is involved in the interaction with other neuronal proteins.
source: Exon 2 is involved in the interaction with other neuronal proteins, and exon 27 facilitates endocytosis of L1CAM (Schäfer and Altevogt, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Schäfer and Altevogt, 2010.

claim: L1CAM exon 27 facilitates endocytosis of L1CAM.
source: Exon 2 is involved in the interaction with other neuronal proteins, and exon 27 facilitates endocytosis of L1CAM (Schäfer and Altevogt, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Schäfer and Altevogt, 2010.

claim: More than 90% of human protein-coding genes undergo alternative splicing.
source: More than 90% of human protein-coding genes undergo AS (Pan et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2008) giving rise to different protein isoforms with distinct structural and functional properties.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Pan et al., 2008 and Wang et al., 2008.

claim: Alternative splicing represents an important mechanism to expand the coding potential of the human genome.
source: Hence, AS represents an important mechanism to expand the coding potential of the human genome, thus contributing to generate the cellular complexity of different tissue types and to support key functional properties (Chen and Manley, 2009; Baralle and Giudice, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chen and Manley, 2009 and Baralle and Giudice, 2017.

claim: Alternative splicing plays a direct role in promoting cancer progression.
source: Notably, several findings highlighted a direct role of AS in promoting cancer progression (Anczuków and Krainer, 2016; Biamonti et al., 2014; Pradella et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Anczuków and Krainer, 2016; Biamonti et al., 2014; and Pradella et al., 2017.

claim: NOVA2 was initially identified in neural cells where it controls alternative splicing of several genes involved in various neural developmental processes.
source: NOVA2 was initially identified in neural cells where it controls AS of several genes involved in various neural developmental processes by binding to clusters of YCAY (Y = C/U) repeats within its pre-mRNA targets (Licatalosi et al., 2008; Ule et al., 2003; Zhang et al., 2010; Leggere et al., 2016; Saito et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Licatalosi et al., 2008; Ule et al., 2003; Zhang et al., 2010; Leggere et al., 2016; and Saito et al., 2016.

claim: NOVA2 is expressed in vascular endothelium and is regulated during angiogenesis.
source: Our study revealed that NOVA2 is also expressed in vascular endothelium and is regulated during angiogenesis (Giampietro et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Giampietro et al., 2015.

claim: NOVA2 controls at the post-transcriptional level the establishment of endothelial cell polarity.
source: NOVA2 controls at the post-transcriptional level the establishment of EC polarity, a process that is essential for vascular lumen formation and, hence, for angiogenesis (Iruela-Arispe and Davis, 2009).
evidence: The claim is based on prior research cited to Iruela-Arispe and Davis, 2009.

claim: NOVA2 ablation causes defects in vascular lumen formation in vivo.
source: Accordingly, NOVA2 ablation causes defects in vascular lumen formation in vivo (Giampietro et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Giampietro et al., 2015.

claim: L1-ΔTM provides the first example of an immunoglobulin-like cell adhesion molecule converted into a soluble angiogenic factor through alternative splicing removal of the exonic sequence that encodes the transmembrane domain.
source: To our knowledge, L1-ΔTM provides the first example of an immunoglobulin-like cell adhesion molecule converted into a soluble angiogenic factor through AS removal of the exonic sequence that encodes the TM domain.
evidence: The claim is a novel finding based on the authors' research.

claim: Extracellular L1-ΔTM can promote angiogenesis via both autocrine and paracrine stimulation.
source: We discovered that ECs acquire angiogenic properties not only upon ectopic expression of L1-ΔTM, but also when exposed to exogenously added L1-ΔTM (either as CM or as a recombinant protein). This supports the notion that extracellular L1-ΔTM can promote angiogenesis via both autocrine and paracrine stimulation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experiments showing angiogenic effects of both cell-expressed and exogenously added L1-ΔTM.

claim: L1CAM frequently engages in homophilic L1CAM-L1CAM interactions between adjacent cells in neurons.
source: In different cellular contexts, such as neurons, L1CAM frequently engages in homophilic L1CAM-L1CAM interactions between adjacent cells, which underlie its function in cell-cell adhesion (Maness and Schachner, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Maness and Schachner, 2007.

claim: L1-ΔTM stimulates endothelial cells by heterophilic interactions with different surface molecules.
source: However, our experiments were conducted in two EC lines, moEC and luEC, that express no or very little endogenous L1CAM. This implies that, regardless of autocrine or paracrine activity, L1-ΔTM stimulates ECs by heterophilic interactions with different surface molecules.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experiments in EC lines with no or low endogenous L1CAM.

claim: The extracellular portion of L1CAM interacts with a wide spectrum of membrane proteins, including different integrins, CD24, NCAM, F11R, and neuropilins.
source: Accordingly, the extracellular portion of L1CAM has been reported to interact with a wide spectrum of membrane proteins, including different integrins, CD24, NCAM, F11R, neuropilins, etc. (Haspel and Grumet, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Haspel and Grumet, 2003.

claim: L1CAM has been proposed to interact with the FGFR signaling machinery in different experimental settings.
source: Following the pioneering studies of Doherty and Walsh in neuronal systems (Williams et al., 1994), L1CAM has been proposed to interact with the FGFR signaling machinery in different experimental settings (Mohanan et al., 2013; Son et al., 2011; Zecchini et al., 2008), possibly entailing a direct binding between the two molecules (Kulahin et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Williams et al., 1994; Mohanan et al., 2013; Son et al., 2011; Zecchini et al., 2008; and Kulahin et al., 2008.

claim: There is a functional interplay between L1-ΔTM and FGFR1 in endothelial cells.
source: Our data show for the first time a functional interplay between L1-ΔTM and FGFR1 in ECs, and implicate it in L1-ΔTM-induced angiogenesis.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' experimental data showing FGFR1 activation and inhibition effects.

claim: In neural cell types, NOVA2 is required for the inclusion of the L1CAM exons 2 and 27.
source: In neural cell types, NOVA2 is required for the inclusion of the L1CAM exons 2 and 27 (Mikulak et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Mikulak et al., 2012.

claim: NOVA2 is not required for the inclusion of L1CAM exons 2 and 27 in endothelial cells.
source: This is not the case in ECs, where even upon ectopic over-expression of NOVA2 exons 2 and 27 are not included in the L1CAM mRNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: L1-ΔTM is not detected in human or mouse brain despite high expression of NOVA2 in the nervous system.
source: Moreover, despite the high expression of NOVA2 in the nervous system (Yano et al., 2010; Giampietro et al., 2015), we did not detect L1-ΔTM in human or mouse brain (Figure 1), which implies that NOVA2 is not involved in the AS of exon 25 in neural cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1 and citations to Yano et al., 2010 and Giampietro et al., 2015.

claim: NOVA2 is significantly up-regulated in ovarian carcinoma vasculature as compared to vessels in healthy ovary.
source: NOVA2 is significantly up-regulated in OC vasculature as compared to vessels in healthy ovary.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data comparing OC and normal ovary.

claim: NOVA2 expression is detected only in the vascular endothelium of ovarian carcinoma.
source: Of note, NOVA2 expression is detected only in the vascular endothelium of OC and, in particular, in the nucleus of ECs.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing nuclear NOVA2 staining in ECs.

claim: NOVA2 has a prognostic value in ovarian carcinoma.
source: It is remarkable that, in spite of such a restricted expression pattern, NOVA2 has a prognostic value in OC, given its association with shorter patients' survival.
evidence: The claim is supported by survival analysis showing correlation between NOVA2 expression and patient outcome.

claim: NOVA2 is the only splicing regulatory factor reported to be upregulated in cancer vasculature.
source: To the best of our knowledge, NOVA2 is the only SRF reported to be upregulated in cancer vasculature, including OC (this study) and colorectal carcinoma (Gallo et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' knowledge and citation to Gallo et al., 2018.

claim: NOVA2-mediated alternative splicing might play a relevant role in the phenotypic and functional aberrancies of tumor vessels.
source: This implies that NOVA2-mediated AS might play a relevant, yet underappreciated, role in the phenotypic and functional aberrancies of the tumor vessels (Carmeliet and Jain, 2011).
evidence: The claim is inferred from NOVA2 upregulation in tumor vasculature and cited to Carmeliet and Jain, 2011.

claim: L1-ΔTM could serve as a new circulating biomarker of cancer-associated vasculature.
source: Based on its specific up-regulation in OC vessels (and likely in other cancer types as well), we speculate that L1-ΔTM could serve as a new circulating biomarker of cancer-associated vasculature.
evidence: The claim is speculative based on the specific expression of L1-ΔTM in tumor vessels.

claim: Circulating L1-ΔTM could be harnessed for diagnostic and prognostic purposes in ovarian carcinoma.
source: Circulating L1-ΔTM could be harnessed for diagnostic and prognostic purposes, ranging from the detection of primary and recurrent OC to monitoring the therapeutic response, all objectives that would improve dramatically the clinical management of OC patients.
evidence: The claim is speculative about potential clinical applications of L1-ΔTM as a biomarker.

claim: Endothelial cells express the non-neural isoform of L1CAM mRNA, which lacks exons 2 and 27.
source: As shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1, ECs express the non-neural isoform of L1CAM mRNA, which lacks exons 2 and 27 (Schäfer and Altevogt, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and citation to Schäfer and Altevogt, 2010.

claim: moEC express no or very little endogenous L1CAM.
source: To test this hypothesis, we selected an immortalized endothelial cell line of murine origin, moEC (Lampugnani et al., 2002; Taddei et al., 2008), because it expresses no or very little endogenous L1CAM (Figure 2B) and, therefore, is amenable to gain-of-function studies.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2B and citations to Lampugnani et al., 2002 and Taddei et al., 2008.

claim: The upper band in L1-FL immunoblot represents the mature, fully glycosylated cell-surface form.
source: Immunoblotting of total extracts from L1-FL-expressing cells showed the expected doublet pattern (Figure 2B), with the upper band representing the mature, fully glycosylated cell-surface form, and the lower band corresponding to the precursor form (Moulding et al., 2000; Zisch et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 2B and citations to Moulding et al., 2000 and Zisch et al., 1997.

claim: The lower band in L1-FL immunoblot corresponds to the precursor form.
source: Immunoblotting of total extracts from L1-FL-expressing cells showed the expected doublet pattern (Figure 2B), with the upper band representing the mature, fully glycosylated cell-surface form, and the lower band corresponding to the precursor form (Moulding et al., 2000; Zisch et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 2B and citations to Moulding et al., 2000 and Zisch et al., 1997.

claim: L1-ΔTM-expressing moEC show a single band that migrates slightly faster than the lower band of L1-FL.
source: In contrast, L1-ΔTM-expressing moEC showed a single band that migrated slightly faster than the lower band of L1-FL (Figure 2B), consistent with the deletion of exon 25.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: moEC express only FGFR1 among the four FGFR family members.
source: Among the four FGFR family members, moEC express only FGFR1 (data not shown) (Giampietro et al., 2012), as previously reported for other EC types (Giacomini et al., 2016; Javerzat et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by unpublished data and citations to Giampietro et al., 2012; Giacomini et al., 2016; and Javerzat et al., 2002.
